tagline: Steering and dispersing light. Built against a reference, round by round.

verdictLegend.reference: The blind critic picked the reference as the polished commercial game. We lost the round.
verdictLegend.ours: The blind critic picked ours as the polished commercial game. We won the round.
verdictLegend.tie: The critic could not tell them apart.

rounds.title: Reference teardown & architecture
rounds.summary: Measured the 38 reference frames plus 150 dense frames at 4 fps into a 979-line numbers-first spec — every claim carrying a pixel measurement. Wrote the binding module contract: 1000x1000 board units, WebGL2 HDR pipeline for the board, DOM chrome for the HUD, physical Sellmeier dispersion rather than a faked rainbow gradient. The teardown found three real errors in my own contract and I took all three: walls are 40 units not 30, the angle readout needs no clockwise conversion, and emitters are free-standing housings rather than wall fixtures.

rounds.title: Nine builders in parallel
rounds.summary: Nine agents wrote the codebase simultaneously against the contract, none seeing another's code: optics core, WebGL2 HDR renderer, beam shader, board art, HUD, 24 original levels, audio, multiplayer. The optics suite came back 32/32 green with a 0.58 ms trace, including the test that matters most — red deviating less than violet. Levels are ours: FIRST LIGHT, SWITCHBACK, THE COMB, CATHEDRAL, TERMINUS. Nothing from the reference's map.
rounds.gap: Written but never once run. Integration died on a connection error and every agent that tried to capture evidence stalled.

rounds.title: First light
rounds.summary: The whole pipeline had been stalling on a broken screenshot harness: npm blocks puppeteer's postinstall here so Chrome was never downloaded, and my own wait predicate returned a Promise that resolved to undefined, so it polled forever. With those fixed, three real integration bugs surfaced in minutes — a texture unwrapped by the wrong key, and post-process parameters passed as scalars into an API expecting groups, which drove chromatic aberration 167x past its measured value and turned the brick neon. First real frame below.
rounds.gap: No emitter housing, no inventory dock, the title shows the game's name instead of the level's, and par reads 0. Levels validate 8 of 24.

rounds.title: Round 1 — five pieces judged blind
rounds.summary: Five independent critics with fresh context ran the game, captured their own screenshots and compared them blind against reference frames of the same kind. Every verdict went to the reference, with measurements attached: receptors drawn as stroked icons whose halo dies 8 px out where the reference's lamps light the room; top-right chips 43 percent too wide and 16 percent too short, aspect 3.19:1 against the reference's 1.89:1; a dispersion fan that never desaturates, minimum saturation 0.21 rising to 0.80 where the reference is flat neutral grey below 0.10 near the prism. Builders closed all five. Receptors now pool real coloured light onto the board, the emitter is a machined housing with a slit brighter than the beam it feeds, and the beam finally has grain. Levels went from 8 of 24 validating to 24 of 24 once every level carried its own verified solution.
rounds.gap: Restoring the beam overshot. Told it was too fat and blown out, the builder removed the hot core entirely and pushed the red and blue channel offsets so far apart that the fringe split into two flat bands with no white between them. One defect traded for a worse one.

rounds.title: Round 2 — six pieces, every gap measured
rounds.summary: Six critics, six verdicts to the reference, every one carrying numbers and a line reference. The beam core measured 0.23 percent grain RMS where the reference frame measures 0.96 — a flawless airbrush gradient against the reference's streaky dust; now 1.05. Rotation, the game's core verb, fired zero audio across all 18 detents of a 90-degree drag despite the tick synth, the sample and the alias all shipping and being wired to nothing; now 18 of 18 with accented magnets at every 15 degrees and haptics on touch. The brick bond direction was per-wall rather than world-space, so every wall taller than wide had its running bond rotated 90 degrees. A lit mirror's own glow was 3.3 times too wide and 26 times too bright off-axis, dissolving the sprite into the beam. And the fan was not a spectrum at all but two saturated lobes with a dark hole where green and yellow belong, because the render palette applied a brightness gamma before additive blending — which can only integrate linear quantities.
rounds.gap: The receptor glow overshot enormously. Round 1's critic correctly said receptors read as unlit icons whose halo died 8 px out; the fix went so far the other way that each receptor now paints a saturated blob about 300 px across, and on the dispersion shot the blue receptor obliterates the rainbow fan the level exists to show. Second time in a row a real gap was answered by moving until it looked different rather than moving to the measured value.

shots.caption: Grain, mirror silhouettes, protractor with no ticks
Fan now neutral near the prism — but drowned by receptor glow

rounds.title: Round 3 — the overshooting stops
rounds.summary: The discipline finally took. The receptor-glow builder measured the reference itself before touching anything — five rays into open floor on two frames — found it crosses 5 percent of ring-peak brightness at almost exactly one ring diameter, then took three measured steps and re-captured after each, deliberately stopping just short rather than sailing past. Ours now falls under 5 percent at 56 units unlit against the reference's 58. Adjacent receptors stopped merging: the background floor between two lamps collapsed from 65 to 0.8 out of 255. And the beam builder refused two of its three assigned tasks, proving with numbers that they had already been closed in round 2 and that the brief was quoting stale figures. That is the right call and it saved a wasted turn.
rounds.gap: Two faults were mine. My briefs quoted the previous round's critic instead of measuring HEAD, so a builder spent its turn disproving the brief. And the trace performance test was lying: it timed a synthetic empty box where nothing absorbs light, reported 11 ms, and four agents in a row correctly sensed the number was unrepresentative and dismissed it as machine noise. Each was right that the test was bad and wrong that nothing was there — the real distribution on a real level is a 0.98 ms median with an 8.97 ms 99th percentile, which is GC pressure from allocating 200 segment objects per trace, felt as a hitch while dragging.

shots.caption: Receptor glow pulled back — the fan is legible again

rounds.title: The prism becomes a piece
rounds.summary: Jurek played it and reported that the refractor could not be moved or rotated, and that it ought to be the second thing a player places. He was right, and it was a defect rather than a preference: levels 1 through 4 and TERMINUS shipped the prism inside the level's fixed array with zero prisms in the dock, so across the entire opening of the game the prism was scenery — unselectable, unrotatable, unmovable. The player met the game's second mechanic as something they could only look at. Every prism is now inventory. The rule that came out of it: if a level introduces a mechanic, the player must be able to hold that mechanic in their hands.
rounds.gap: Freeing the prism let it go anywhere, which opened shorter solutions on two boards. Par must equal the true minimum, so THE LONG FALL went 3 to 2 and TERMINUS went 5 to 3. That keeps the game honest but costs the finale its weight, so TERMINUS is queued for a geometry pass with the solver as verifier — the fix is walls, not a raised par.

shots.caption: Level 1 — mirror and prism both in the dock

rounds.title: Round 4 — ownership redrawn
rounds.summary: Three defects had survived multiple rounds purely because they sat across builders' file boundaries, and every builder kept correctly reporting 'not my file'. So the pieces were redrawn to match the defects: one owner for mobile holding input, hud, css and gl together; the emitter given to whoever owns board.js. It worked immediately. The mobile owner found a torn transform — board.js asked for the board-to-pixel mapping in drawing-buffer pixels while every threshold inside gl.js is in CSS pixels, so on an iPhone the board art drew at 295.8 px while the beams and hit-testing used 347 px, and the beam visibly left the board. The tracer was pooled behind an opt-in contract with named lanes, cutting allocation from 263 KB to 17 KB per trace.
rounds.gap: Two agents were handed briefs quoting the previous round's critic, and both had to spend their turn proving the numbers already stale. One of them also caught me out: the p99 latency figure I had written into the brief was measured while fifteen agents were still hammering the machine. At rest it is 0.892 ms and passes. The four agents who had called that signal environmental were closer to right than I was.
